clue.text: Educated hero has rank and name on memorial

indicators.note: the rank and name are written after, as if inscribed on, the memorial

parts.note: a tomb is a monument to the dead
a row, as in a rank of soldiers

explanation.surface: A schoolboy hero's name and rank are carved on a war memorial.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Brown is the hero of Thomas Hughes's Victorian novel Tom Brown's Schooldays, set at Rugby School, which fits the puzzle's school theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Tom Brown's Schooldays is a fictional hero whose schooling is the whole story.

clue.text: Teaching unit showing word, clause and sentence

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a division of the school year
second meaning: a word or expression
third meaning: a condition in a contract
fourth meaning: a period of imprisonment

explanation.walkthrough: Four separate meanings of one short word; the grammar words word, clause and sentence look like a set but each points to a different sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names a school period, a vocabulary item, a contractual condition and a stretch in prison.

clue.text: Mother's framing son's degree

indicators.note: the mother's word sits around the son, like a frame round a picture

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, an old public-school word for one's mum, so mater's is mother's
S for son; the 's stands for is, linking wordplay to definition

explanation.surface: A proud mother has her son's degree certificate framed.
explanation.walkthrough: Mater was public-school slang for mother. The 's of son's is read as is, joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A master's is a postgraduate university qualification, such as an MA or MSc.

clue.text: In secret, children bring up unpleasant matter

indicators.note: the answer is found lying inside the run of letters of the next two words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of secret and the start of children

explanation.surface: Children secretly raise distasteful topics among themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bring up unpleasant matter' reads like airing an awkward subject, but it is literal: heaving as if about to be sick.
explanation.definitionFit: To retch is to make the motions of vomiting, trying to expel the stomach's contents.

clue.text: Going to collect law degree in comfort

indicators.note: the going word gathers the law degree into its middle

parts.note: weeing, i.e. going to the toilet, a childish word for urinating
LLB, Bachelor of Laws

explanation.surface: Someone heads off to pick up their law degree in a comfortable state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going' looks like travelling but is the toilet sense of going. LLB is the usual abbreviation for a Bachelor of Laws degree.
explanation.definitionFit: Wellbeing is a state of health, ease and contentment, much as comfort is.

clue.text: Head of house punching towny in trouble all right

indicators.note: the house letter breaks into the middle of the jumbled word, as a fist punches in
the word towny is in a mess, its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written; a towny is a townsperson, as opposed to a student

indicators.note: only the first letter of the word house is taken

parts.note: its first letter is the head of the word

explanation.surface: A head of house thumps a local lad in a town-and-gown brawl, and calls it fine.
explanation.walkthrough: Head of house sounds like a school prefect, but only supplies the first letter of house. Towny is the old student word for a non-university local.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying why not agrees to a suggestion, much like answering okay or sure.

clue.text: Public school changing hands seen leaderless, a scary time

indicators.note: each right hand, R, is swapped for a left, L

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public (private fee-paying) school

indicators.note: the word seen loses its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A public school goes through a change of ownership, unseen and without a leader, at a frightening time.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are right and left, so changing hands swaps one for the other. Harrow is an English public school, which in Britain means a private one.
explanation.definitionFit: Halloween, on 31 October, is the night of ghosts, costumes and frights.

clue.text: Needing A, approach course like a swot

indicators.note: the approach word is in need of, i.e. missing, the letter A

parts.note: to near is to approach
the letter A, taken as written, is what the approach word lacks
a dish is a course of a meal

explanation.surface: A pupil who needs an A grade approaches the course like a dedicated swot.
explanation.walkthrough: A swot is British slang for a pupil who studies too hard. 'Needing A' reads as wanting a top grade, but tells you the A is absent.
explanation.definitionFit: Nerdish means studious and socially awkward, the image of a pupil who swots.

clue.text: Fractions passed in test Henry and I smashed

indicators.note: the passed word sits within the jumbled letters
the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
went, as in passed or travelled

explanation.surface: Henry and I passed the test with flying colours, smashing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashed' reads as a slang word for succeeding brilliantly, but signals jumbled letters. H is the symbol for henry, the unit of inductance.
explanation.definitionFit: A twentieth is one of twenty equal parts, so twentieths are fractions of a whole.

clue.text: Pass back for smallest young sportsman

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass

indicators.note: the back end of smallest supplies its last letter

parts.note: its final letter is the back of the word

explanation.surface: A tiny young player makes a backward pass in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass back' looks like a football move, but pass is a mountain col and back belongs to the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A colt is a young, inexperienced player, especially in a junior cricket or rugby team.

clue.text: Second attempt, others taking one

indicators.note: the others word takes in the letter for one

parts.note: the rest means the others

explanation.surface: On a second go, the rest of the class take one more exam.
explanation.walkthrough: I is the Roman numeral for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A resit is an examination taken again after failing it, a second try.

clue.text: Facilities spread around school finally seem important

parts.note: a loo is the toilet, euphemistically the facilities

indicators.note: the spread is placed around a single letter

parts.note: marge, short for margarine, a spread for bread

indicators.note: only the last letter of school is used

parts.note: the word ends in L, its final letter

explanation.surface: The school's toilets are being expanded, which finally looks significant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread' seems to be a verb about enlarging the facilities, but it is a noun: marge, the British short form of margarine.
explanation.definitionFit: To loom large is to appear threatening or significant, to dominate one's attention.

clue.text: Show-off with scholarship is last in sport

parts.note: an exhibition is a type of scholarship awarded at some schools and universities
taken as written

indicators.note: only the final letter of sport is taken

parts.note: the word ends in T, its last letter

explanation.surface: A boastful pupil on a scholarship comes last in games.
explanation.walkthrough: An exhibition is a financial award to a student, usually smaller than a full scholarship, at British schools and colleges.
explanation.definitionFit: An exhibitionist is someone who behaves extravagantly to attract attention to themselves.

clue.text: Drink something to prevent dry mouth in school presentation

indicators.note: the drink and spit sit inside the school abbreviation

parts.note: ale is a beer
spit, saliva, keeps the mouth moist

explanation.surface: Someone takes a drink to stop their mouth drying up during a talk at school.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase looks like a lozenge or a glass of water before a speech, but it means spit itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A sales pitch is a persuasive talk aimed at selling something, a kind of presentation.

clue.text: Hit two dunces by gates out of bounds

parts.note: an ass is a fool, so two of them
in, as in by the hour meaning in hours, or by day meaning in the day

indicators.note: the word gates loses its boundary letters, its first and last

parts.note: with its two outer letters, the bounds, removed, the inside of the word is left

explanation.surface: Two dim pupils who were gated are caught out of bounds and hit.
explanation.walkthrough: Hit is the gangland sense: to kill someone to order. Being gated was school punishment, confinement to school, so out of bounds fits the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In criminal slang a hit is a contract killing, so to hit someone is to murder them.

clue.text: Submit trouble ensued with three Rs

indicators.note: the letters are troubled, i.e. stirred up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
three copies of the letter R

explanation.surface: A pupil gives in after trouble followed over the three Rs, reading, writing and arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: The three Rs, reading, writing and arithmetic, are the basics of schooling; here they are just three letter Rs.
explanation.definitionFit: To surrender is to give up or yield, to submit to another's power.

clue.text: Consequences if learner leaves at half-term, cycling

indicators.note: letters are moved round from the front of the string to the back

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the learner departs, taking its letter out of the word

parts.note: taken as written, without its hyphen
L, as on a learner driver's L-plate

explanation.surface: If a student drops out over half-term and goes cycling, there will be consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-term is the short school holiday in the middle of a British term. After the L goes, the string starting at is cycled round until it reads as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An aftermath is the period of consequences following an event, especially an unpleasant one.

clue.text: Hurry up, coming from lecturer

indicators.note: what comes out of a lecturer's mouth is speech, so the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: high, as in up above

explanation.surface: A lecturer tells the class to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hurry up' looks like a single phrase, but up belongs to the wordplay. Hie is an archaic word for go quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Hie is an old poetic verb meaning to hasten or go quickly.

clue.text: Exam beginner misses is in Latin

indicators.note: the exam's beginning letter is missed out

parts.note: a test

explanation.surface: A first-year pupil misses an exam in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginner' looks like a novice pupil, but it is the first letter of the exam word.
explanation.definitionFit: Est is the third-person singular present of the Latin verb esse, meaning to be.

clue.text: English dons translated Proust for companies

indicators.note: dons means puts on, so the jumbled name takes on the English letter like donning a garment
Proust is changed into a different form, its letters rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: English university lecturers have rendered Proust into their own language.
explanation.walkthrough: Dons looks like university teachers, but here it is the verb: puts on.
explanation.definitionFit: Troupes are companies of actors or performers who work together.

clue.text: Certainly worth a mark?

definitions.meaning: a mainly Scottish phrase for certainly, sure enough
read cryptically as an answer correct enough to be marked right, earning a tick

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means indeed, but read literally it describes a pupil's answer that is right enough to earn a mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Right enough is an idiom for indeed or undoubtedly, and its literal reading suits a marked answer.

clue.text: Posh youth grabs hold of member, a lot

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing in for an adjective of number: umpteen means very many

indicators.note: the posh youth clutches the member in its middle

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in the U and non-U usage of the 1950s
a teen, a teenager
MP, Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A well-bred teenager latches on to an MP, and quite a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class comes from Nancy Mitford's U and non-U, a famous essay on British class markers.
explanation.definitionFit: Umpteen is an informal word for an indefinitely large number, many.

clue.text: Teaching post is for prep schools in odd places, supply

indicators.note: read as the adverb of supple: the letters bend into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: only the letters in the first, third, fifth and seventh positions of schools are used

parts.note: reading only the odd-numbered letters of the word

explanation.surface: A teaching job is advertised to supply prep schools in various odd places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like supply teaching, but it is supple plus -ly, bending the letters into shape. A prep school is a British private school for younger children.
explanation.definitionFit: A professorship is the post held by a university professor, a senior academic teaching position.

clue.text: Ego depressed by teacher's voice on the phone

indicators.note: in a down clue the ego is pushed down beneath the teacher

parts.note: Sir is what pupils call a male teacher; the 's stands for is
I, the self

explanation.surface: A pupil's sense of self is crushed by a teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: Pupils in Britain address a male teacher as Sir. In a down answer, one piece depressed by another lies below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Siri is Apple's voice assistant, the speaking voice on an iPhone.

clue.text: Choice offered by tosser in the toilets

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... or tails, the call when someone tosses a coin
second meaning: on a ship the toilets are called the ...

explanation.walkthrough: Tosser looks like an insult but is just someone tossing a coin; heads is also naval slang for toilets.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin-toss offers heads or tails, and sailors call a ship's lavatories the heads.

clue.text: Male cuts evidence of where he went to school up in shed

indicators.note: in a down answer the whole is read upwards, from bottom to top
the male letter cuts into the middle of the tie

parts.words: evidence of where he went to school
parts.note: an old school tie shows which school a man attended

explanation.surface: A man wearing his old school tie cuts something up in a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like a garden hut but is a verb, to give off, as a lamp sheds light. The old school tie is a British emblem of a man's school.
explanation.definitionFit: To emit is to give out or send forth, as when light or heat is shed.

clue.text: Some translate Pindar iambs, scratching note in classicists' bathrooms

indicators.note: scratching out, deleting, the note letter from the poet's name

parts.note: some of the letters of these words: the run straddling the end of translate, all of Pindar and the start of iambs
N, a note in the sense of n for a musical or written note abbreviation

explanation.surface: Classics pupils translate the poet Pindar's verse in Roman bathhouses, crossing out notes.
explanation.walkthrough: Some signals a run of letters lying inside the three words; scratching then removes the note letter. Pindar was an ancient Greek poet and iambs are metrical feet; tepidaria are the warm rooms of Roman baths.
explanation.definitionFit: A tepidarium was the warm room in a Roman bath complex, between the hot and cold rooms.

clue.text: 1st XI in the morning takes break from cricket

indicators.note: the morning letters take the break inside them

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem
tea is the interval between the afternoon sessions of a cricket match

explanation.surface: The school's first eleven stop for tea in the morning during a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: A first-class cricket match pauses for lunch and tea. The 1st XI is a school's top cricket team of eleven players.
explanation.definitionFit: The A team is the first or best team, just as the 1st XI is a school's top side.

clue.text: Big player in games keeps ball rolling

parts.note: has, as in holds or possesses

indicators.note: the ball word rolls over, reading backwards

parts.note: an orb, a sphere

explanation.surface: A key player in a sports match keeps the ball moving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big player in games' looks like a star athlete, but means a major company in the games trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Hasbro is a major American toy and board-game company, maker of Monopoly and Scrabble.

clue.text: Reddish-brown uniform packed in trunk with books

parts.note: a chest, a large box for storage

indicators.note: the uniform letter is packed into the other letters

parts.note: NT, the New Testament books of the Bible
U, uniform in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A school uniform of reddish-brown is packed in a trunk with the books for the new term.
explanation.walkthrough: Uniform is U in the NATO phonetic alphabet, and NT, the New Testament, is a standard crossword source for books.
explanation.definitionFit: Chestnut is the reddish-brown colour of the nut's shell, also used of horses and hair.
